the *A. oryzae* genome. In addition, the finding that a large number of pectinolytic genes exist in the *A. oryzae* genome suggests that *A. oryzae* might have originated from wild plant pathogens such as *A. flavus*, and thus might have a number of plant cell-wall degrading enzymes.

In contrast, another noteworthy feature of *A. oryzae* hydrolytic genes is an apparent decrease in the number of genes with a cellulose-binding domain (CBD) or a starch-binding domain (SBD). Fungal cellulases often contain a CBD in either the N- or the C-terminal region of the protein, and this has been shown to increase cellulolytic activity toward insoluble cellulose.<sup>32)</sup> Also, some amylolytic enzymes, such as $\alpha$-amylase and glucoamylase, contain an SBD, which allows an amylase to bind and efficiently digest raw, granular starch.<sup>33)</sup> Whereas *N. crassa* has 19 genes with a CBD, *A. oryzae* has only five CBD-containing genes, among which one gene, coding for a protein with similarity to $\beta$-mannanase of *A. aculeatus*, contains a CBD at the N-terminus. Most enzymes isolated so far from Aspergilli have a CBD in the C-terminal region of the protein, but in the *A. oryzae* genome there exists a gene encoding a protein with a CBD at the N-terminus, which suggests that hydrolytic enzymes with a CBD at the N-terminus commonly exist in other Aspergilli. On the other hand, the black Aspergilli *A. niger* and *A. kawachii* have been found to have an $\alpha$-amylase with an SBD, and also to have at least one glucoamylase with an SBD, but only

one glucoamylase gene (*glaA*) exists in *A. oryzae* as an SBD-containing amylase. The $\alpha$-amylase with an SBD in the black Aspergilli is an acid-stable $\alpha$-amylase, which is highly homologous to Taka-amylase A in its catalytic domain, and can digest raw starch efficiently.<sup>34)</sup> In contrast to the black Aspergilli, no gene coding for $\alpha$-amylase with an SBD has been found in *A. oryzae*. Conversely, to date, other Aspergilli have no ortholog of *A. oryzae glaB*, encoding glucoamylase without an SBD, which is specifically expressed when grown on steamed rice grains.<sup>26)</sup> Taken together, comparative study appears to support the hypothesis<sup>35)</sup> that *A. oryzae* is a domesticated fungus derived evolutionarily from a wild plant pathogenic species, *A. flavus*, although *A. oryzae* is now considered to be non-pathogenic. Furthermore, *A. oryzae* has perhaps lost cellulolytic and amylolytic enzymes with a substrate-binding domain during domestication, because it is not necessary for the fungus to digest insoluble cellulose or raw starch in the fermented food production process.

## 2. Proteolytic enzymes

Proteolytic enzymes that hydrolyze peptide bonds include endopeptidases and exopeptidases.<sup>36,37)</sup> Endopeptidases are classified into several groups according to catalytic mechanisms. Therefore, the conserved amino acid sequences around the catalytic residues (motifs) have been used to identify the endopeptidase genes in the *A. oryzae* genome (Table 1). Exopeptidases are classified by the mode of action into aminopeptidases, dipeptidases, dipeptidyl or tripeptidyl peptidases, and carboxypeptidases. *A. oryzae* exopeptidase genes have been identified as genes with significant matches (COG scores above 150) with known exopetidases in public databases.

To date, the amino acid and/or nucleotide sequences of the peptidases of *A. oryzae* have been reported for only 18 enzymes. However, the genome sequence of *A. oryzae* has revealed the existence of 134 peptidase genes, consisting of 69 exopeptidases and 65 endopeptidases, in the organism (Table 2). This number is strikingly larger than those for other fungi, even compared to other *Aspergillus* species such as *A. nidulans* and *A. fumigatus*.<sup>2)</sup> The peptidase genes occupy roughly 1% of total genes in the *A. oryzae* genome. It is noteworthy that homologs of secreted peptidases that act at acidic pH, such as aspartic proteinase, pepstatin insensitive protease, aorsin, and serine-type carboxy-

peptidase, are numerous in the *A. oryzae* genome. This is probably because the growth of *A. oryzae* is adapted to acidic pH conditions. *A. oryzae* has 12 cysteine endopetidase genes, but no papain-like cysteine endopeptidase gene is present, confirming the previous suggestion that *Aspergillus* species do not produce papain-like enzymes to the culture broth. Although only four aspartic endopeptidase (EC 3.4.23.18) genes<sup>38–40)</sup> and one serine-type carboxypeptidase (EC 3.4.16.-) gene<sup>41)</sup> have been cloned and sequenced to date, there are 12 serine-type carboxypeptidase genes and 11 aspartic endopeptidase genes in the *A. oryzae* genome. Among these, seven serine-type carboxypeptidase genes and eight aspartic endopeptidase genes are present in the EST data base of *A. oryzae*. *A. oryzae* also has many metalloproteinase genes. Half of the metalloproteinases and most of the aspartic proteinases and the serine-type carboxypeptidases have a typical signal sequence, suggesting that these enzymes are secreted enzymes. As to intracellular proteinases, there are four insulinase genes, seven ubiquitin-specific protease genes, and six ATP dependent proteinase genes. None of these genes has a homolog in the *A. oryzae* genome, suggesting that each of them has a distinctive physiological role.

Three pairs of highly homologous genes are present in each of the serine-type carboxypeptidases, metalloendopeptidases, and aspartic proteinases, and most of the pairs share the same number of introns. As an example, the phylogenetic tree of the aspartic endopeptidases is shown (Fig. 6). The genes in each pair (A, B, and C) have homology of 60–86%, and they have the identical number of introns at identical positions. However, none of them appears to be a pseudogene, since they are dispersed in the *A. oryzae* genome and they possess completely conserved active site motifs. The highly homologous pairs must have emerged by relatively recent gene duplication. The reason *A. oryzae* has so many secreted peptidase genes might also be explained by gene duplication occurred in the distant past. In any case, the abundance of secreted peptidases suggests that *A. oryzae* must have been selected as a high producer of secreted peptidases for fermentation of proteinous materials such as soybean.

# III. Transcription Factors

### 1. Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> transcription factors

Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> binuclear cluster DNA-binding proteins are transcriptional activators specific to fungi.<sup>43)</sup> Most of them bind to an inverted, everted, or direct repeat of CGG separated by an unconserved short spacing sequence. Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors usually act as pathway-specific activators that respond to a small molecular weight inducer to coordinate expression of structural genes of related function. Genes under the control of the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors include those for utilization of carbon and nitrogen sources, and those for biosynthesis of primary and secondary metabolites. The prototype of Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors is Gal4p of *S. cerevisiae*, which activates transcription of galactose utilization genes in response to galactose.<sup>44)</sup> As is to be expected from the variety of utilizable carbon and nitrogen sources in nature and of primary and secondary metabolites produced, Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors constitute the largest family among the transcription factors found in fungi.

Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors must possess at least three functional domains, *viz.* DNA binding, transcriptional activation, and signal sensing domains, to perform signal-dependent transcriptional activation. To date, no conserved motif has been established for the activation domain in this family, and the signal-sensing domain must be unconserved since each factor responds to a different signal. The DNA binding domain contains the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> motif, which has been used to identify transcription factors in this family in the *A. oryzae* genome. In addition, the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors have a relatively well-conserved domain called a middle homology domain of unknown function. Therefore, proteins with the middle homology domain and/or with significant homology to the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors in other organisms have been examined manually.

*S. cerevisiae* possesses 53 genes encoding the proteins of this family, while *N. crassa* has 77 open reading frames with the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> motif.<sup>45)</sup> Compared to these organisms, *A. oryzae* possesses many more Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors, 187. Since the number of proteins with the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> motif is also high in *A. nidulans*, expansion of Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors might be characteristic of the genus *Aspergillus*. Considering that most of these factors characterized to date are involved in the regulation of metabolic genes, the expansion of the Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors appears consistent with the expansion of metabolic genes described above. Another noteworthy observation on this family is that over 30% of *A. oryzae* Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> genes have no obvious orthologs in *A. nidulans*. These factors unique to *A. oryzae* might control expression of *A. oryzae*-specific genes.

Among the genes coding for *A. oryzae* Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors, only 39 genes are significantly homologous with E-values below $10 \times 10^{-30}$ to the 20 genes already known. The difference in gene numbers is due to the existence of homologous genes within the *A. oryzae* genome. For example, *A. oryzae* has five and three homologs of *S. cerevisiae* Rdr1p<sup>46)</sup> and Gal4p respectively, and three and three homologs of *A. nidulans* UaY<sup>47)</sup> and NirA<sup>48)</sup> respectively. These homologs must have emerged by gene duplication, but it is not known whether they have overlapping functions. Consequently, we can refer reliably to the physiological functions of only 19 *A. oryzae* Zn(II)<sub>2</sub>Cys<sub>6</sub> factors out of the 187 (Table 3); seven factors have been cloned from *A. oryzae*, and the other 12 factors have an obvious ortholog each characterized in other fungi. Most of these regulate carbon or nitrogen metabolism, except that PRO1 and RosA are involved in sexual development,<sup>49,50)</sup> and Rdr1p is a repressor of drug-resistance genes.<sup>46)</sup>

AmyR is a transcriptional activator for amylolytic genes in *Aspergillus*.<sup>28,51,52)</sup> AmyR-mediated transcription is controlled by regulation of its nuclear localization (Kobayashi, unpublished) in response to the physiological inducer isomaltose in *A. nidulans*.<sup>53)</sup> The *amyR* gene is clustered with *agdA* and *amyA* genes encoding $\alpha$-glucosidase and $\alpha$-amylase in both *A. oryzae* and *A. nidulans*. Deletion of the *amyR* gene causes significant defects in growth on both maltose and starch in *A. nidulans*,<sup>52)</sup> but only on starch in *A. oryzae* (Gomi, unpublished), suggesting that the genes under the control of AmyR differ slightly in *A. nidulans* and *A. oryzae*. Probably, *A. oryzae* has an $\alpha$-glucosidase(s) regulated by a transcription factor other than AmyR. A candidate for such a transcription factor is MalR, the gene for which forms a cluster similar to the *S. cerevisiae MAL* cluster<sup>54)</sup> with an $\alpha$-glucosidase and a maltose permease gene (Gomi, unpublished). *A. nidulans* possesses an orthologous cluster but, interestingly, expression of the $\alpha$-glucosidase gene in the cluster is AmyR-dependent (Kobayashi, unpublished). An ortholog of the *SugR* gene of *A. parasiticus* might also be related to $\alpha$-linked-sugar utilization, since *SugR* is clustered with an $\alpha$-glucosidase and a hexose transporter gene.<sup>55)</sup> AoXlnR<sup>56)</sup> is an ortholog of *A. niger* XlnR.<sup>57)</sup> It

## 2. C2H2 transcription factors

C2H2 transcription factors are found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, and they constitute the second-largest family in the filamentous fungus *N. crassa*.<sup>1)</sup> Compared to Zn(II)₂Cys₆ factors, the C2H2 factors so far characterized are involved in the regulation of a larger number of genes, and hence they are more crucial to the life of filamentous fungi.

In the *A. oryzae* genome, there are 64 ORFs with the C2H2 zinc finger motif, making the second largest family of transcription factors, as in the *N. crassa* genome. The number of genes in this family in *A. oryzae* is much larger than that in *N. crassa* (43 factors). With regard to other *Aspergillus* species, there are 69 and 64 factors in the *A. nidulans* and *A. fumigatus* genomes respectively, suggesting that the genes in this family are enriched in *Aspergillus* genomes. In *A. oryzae*, three genes in this family, *creA*, *brlA*, and *pacC*, have been deposited in DNA databases, and among these only the *brlA* gene has been characterized to

## 3. GATA factors

GATA factors that bind to (A/T)GATA(A/G) motifs are found only in eukaryotic organisms. There are six genes encoding GATA factors in the *A. oryzae* genome (Table 5). The number of the GATA factors is conserved among *N. crassa*, *A. nidulans*, and *A. fumigatus*, suggesting that filamentous fungi share an identical composition of GATA factors with each other. Among the six GATA factors, only the *areA* gene, which is an ortholog of *A. nidulans areA* and is involved in nitrogen metabolism, has been cloned and characterized from *A. oryzae*.<sup>83)</sup> Each of the three other *A. oryzae* GATA factors has an obvious ortholog characterized in *A. nidulans*. ## IV. Cell Signaling

### 4. Other transcription factors

Living cells, including fungi, are equipped with mechanisms for sensing various environmental stimuli, such as osmotic stress, oxidative stress, and pheromones, which allow adaptation to stimuli through a variety of cellular responses triggered by the sensing and subsequent signaling systems. Filamentous fungi, including the three *Aspergillus* species *A. oryzae*, *A. nidulans*, and *A. fumigatus*, are more tolerant to various conditions than yeasts, and hence they are expected to possess extensive networks for sensing and signaling. Analysis of genome information on the three *Aspergillus* species indicates that the organization of the sensing and signal transduction systems, and in particular of the upstream signaling machinery (G-protein coupled receptors, G-protein $\alpha$ subunits G$\alpha$, two-component signaling proteins, etc.) is more complex than that found in yeasts (Fig. 7). Among the predicted signaling systems, this

*A. oryzae* possesses 10 predicted helix-loop-helix (HLH) proteins, which were first discovered in mammals.<sup>89)</sup> None of the *A. oryzae* HLH factors has been characterized to date. In *A. nidulans*, two factors with the HLH motif have been reported. One is PenR2, involved in the repression of penicillin synthesis,<sup>90)</sup> and the other is DevR, involved in conidiophore development.<sup>91)</sup>

# 1. Two-component signaling

Two-component signaling genes. Two-component systems (or His-to-Asp phosphorelays), first described in bacteria, are a widely spread signal-transduction mechanism in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. The systems consist of three types of common signal transducers: a sensor with histidine kinase activity, a response regulator containing a phospho-accepting receiver, and a histidine-containing phospho-transmitter (HPt). In addition to precisely examined bacterial systems, two-component systems are also well-characterized in eukaryotic microorganisms such as *S. cerevisiae* and *Shizosaccharomyces pombe*. These organisms have only a small number of common signal transducers as compared to prokaryotes: one histidine kinase, two response regulators, and one HPt in *S. cerevisiae*, but three histidine kinases, two response regulators, and one HPt in *S. pombe*. The yeast systems are involved in osmotic and oxidative stress responses, and also in regulation of the mitotic cell cycle and sexual development. In contrast to the yeast systems, a filamentous fungus, *N. crassa*, possesses more divergent signaling pathways, including 11 histidine kinases, two response regulators, and one Hpt.<sup>1)</sup> Genome analysis of the three *Aspergillus* species has revealed that they possess more redundant histidine kinases than *N. crassa* (Table 6). This divergence suggests the importance of the two component systems for the three *Aspergillus* species in responding to environmental stimuli.

Histidine kinases in Aspergillus. Two histidine kinase genes, *tcsA* and *tcsB*, have been reported in *A. nidulans*.<sup>95,96)</sup> The *tcsA* gene is required for sporulation under normal osmotic conditions, while the *tcsB* gene is a homolog of *S. cerevisiae SLN1*. The *FOS-1* gene of *A. fumigatus*, involved in cell-wall assembly, is the ortholog of *tcsA*.<sup>97)</sup> In addition to the *tcsA* and *tcsB* genes, *A. nidulans* possesses 13 putative histidine kinase genes, while *A. oryzae* and *A. fumigatus* possess 13 and 11 histidine kinase genes respectively, in addition to the *tcsA* and *tcsB* orthologs (Table 6). Based on amino acid sequence similarity, *Aspergillus* histidine kinases can be classified into nine families (HK1–9). Except for HK6 and HK8, each family is simply composed of orthologs. No orthologs or paralogs that correspond to *N. crassa* NCU02057.1, NCU09520.1, NCU03164.1, or NCU00939.1 are present in the three *Aspergillus* species.

The histidine kinase genes of the plant pathogens *Cochliobolus heterostrophus*, *Gibberella moniliformis*, and *Botryotinia fuckeliana* have been classified into 11 groups.<sup>98)</sup> Group I, consisting of *N. crassa* NCU09520 and its paralogs, and group XI, consisting of NCU00939.1, NCU03164.1, and their paralogs, are highly divergent within each group. Interestingly, the three *Aspergillus* species do not possess any histidine kinases classified into these groups, supporting the suggestion by Catlett *et al.*<sup>98)</sup> that these groups contain paralogs required for virulence. In addition, group II histidine kinases are absent in the *Aspergillus* species. In contrast, HK8 histidine kinases are specific to the *Aspergillus* species. Family HK8 is highly divergent internally, and contains seven, five, and five histidine kinases of *A. nidulans*, *A. oryzae*, and *A. fumigatus* respectively. Families HK1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 are conserved among *Aspergillus*, *Neurospora*, and the plant pathogens.

Possible roles of Aspergillus histidine kinases. Family HK1 is composed of orthologs of *A. nidulans tcsB*. TcsB is a possible transmembrane osmosensor histidine kinase, because it is highly homologous to the osmosensor Sln1p of *S. cerevisiae*, and overexpression of *tcsB* cDNA can suppress the lethality of a temperature-sensitive osmosensing-defective *sln1-ts* mutant.<sup>95)</sup> *A. nidulans* and other *Aspergillus* species might have more complex osmoregulatory systems than *S. cerevisiae*, since the *A. nidulans tcsB* disruptant does not exhibit any detectable phenotypic defects on standard and stress media.

Family HK3 contains *A. nidulans tcsA* and *A. fumigatus FOS-1*. The *tcsA* disruptant does not produce conidia on standard *Aspergillus* media, but this defect is suppressed by growth on 1 M sorbitol.<sup>96)</sup> TcsA regulates nuclear localization of DevR, a transcription factor with the HLH motif involved in the development of *A. nidulans*.<sup>91)</sup> The *FOS-1* disruptant does not exhibit a detectable defect in either hyphal growth or morphology on solid media,<sup>97)</sup> but conidiophore development is delayed in liquid media as compared to the wild type. A possible role of FOS-1p in the regulation of cell-wall assembly has been suggested, since the disruptant is highly resistant to dicarboximide fungicides and Novozym 234.

*S. pombe* has three histidine kinases, *phk1/mak2*, *phk2/mak3*, and *phk3/mak1*, all of which are involved

in oxidative stress response, mitotic cell cycle control, and sexual development.<sup>99–101)</sup> *phk1/mak2* and *phk2/mak3* are homologous to each other, while *phk3/mak1* is phylogenetically different from the others. The former two correspond to HK4 members, and the latter corresponds to HK5 members. This imply that *Aspergillus* species share a signaling pathway similar to that of *S. pombe*.

The members of HK6 are orthologs and paralogs of *N. crassa* Nik-1. Disruption of the *nik-1<sup>+</sup>* gene results in swollen and misshapen aerial hyphae that appear to lyse.<sup>102)</sup> The growth of the disruptant on solid medium is extremely restricted under conditions of high osmopressure, implying that HK6 histidine kinases are essential for growth in environments with high osmotic pressure. An Nik-1 ortholog is present in all *Aspergillus* species as well as the plant pathogens. All these fungi possess only a single HK6 histidine kinase, except that *A. oryzae* possesses two additional paralogs. Since *A. oryzae* produces extremely high amounts of $\alpha$-amylase, the hydrolysis rate of starch exceeds the consumption rate of the produced oligosaccharides and glucose. When the organism is grown on steamed rice to make koji, a solid-state starter culture in sake brewery, the osmotic pressure of the microenvironments surrounding the mycelia should increase significantly. Repetitive culturing under such high-osmolarity conditions may have led *A. oryzae* to acquire additional Nik-1 paralogs.

Family HK7 is composed of phytochrome homologs that are most similar to bacteriophytochromes, and may have a role in sensing red light. Each *Aspergillus* species has a single putative phytochrome-like histidine kinase. Since exposure to red light is required for abundant conidia formation in *veA<sup>+</sup> A. nidulans* strains, the HK7 gene in *A. nidulans* might function as a red light sensor upstream of VeA.

The physiological roles of the other HK families, including *Aspergillus* specific HK8, remain to be clarified.

*HPt.* While 13 to 15 histidine kinases are present, only a single *HPt* gene is present in the *Aspergillus* species, as observed in *N. crassa* and the plant pathogens. *A. nidulans* HPt can suppress defects in the *S. cerevisiae* YPD1 mutant (Abe *et al.*, unpublished). The question arises whether all the histidine kinases transmit a signal to a single HPt.

*Response regulators.* At present, two response regulator genes, *srrA* and *sskA*, in *A. nidulans* are in the public databases. Except that *A. nidulans* possesses an additional response regulator gene, *Aspergillus* species have only two response regulators, which correspond to *S. cerevisiae* Skn7p and Skk1p, or *S. pombe* Prr1 and Mcs4/Spy1. *A. nidulans sskA* can suppress the defects caused by a mutation in the *S. cerevisiae* counterpart (Abe *et al.*, unpublished). As described above, *Aspergillus* species possess Sln1p-like histidine kinase (HK1), which responds to high osmolarity signals, as well as Phk1/2/3 (Mak1/2/3)-like histidine kinases (HK4 and

5), which respond to oxidative stress. How the signals caused by high osmolarity and oxidative stress are separated is currently unknown. Scaffolding proteins and/or modulation of activities of signaling molecules might increase the selectivity of the signaling pathways.

## 2. MAP kinase cascades

*MAP kinase pathways.* Mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase pathways are highly conserved signaling units found in eukaryotes, where they play essential roles in the response to environmental signals and hormones, growth factors, and cytokines. MAP kinase pathways control cell growth, morphogenesis, proliferation, and stress responses, and they are involved in many disease processes.<sup>103)</sup>

Central to each MAP kinase pathway are three tiers of protein kinases, a MAP kinase (MAPK), a MAP kinase kinase (MAPKK) or MEK, and a MAP kinase kinase kinase (MAPKKK) or MEKK (Fig. 8). MAPKKK phosphorylates and thereby activates MAPKK on serine and threonine within a conserved part at the N-terminal lobe of the kinase domain. Subsequently, MAPKK phosphorylates the MAP kinase on a threonine (sometimes serine) and tyrosine residue, which are located adjacent to each other, separated by a single amino acid (T/S-X-Y). The phosphorylation site is located in the activation loop of the catalytic domain; dual phosphorylation on threonine and tyrosine is necessary for activation of the MAP kinase. Typically, phosphorylation stimulates transfer of the MAP kinase from the cytosol to the nucleus, where it phosphorylates targets on serine/threonine followed by a proline. A portion of activated MAP kinase is apparently also present in the cytoplasm to mediate posttranslational effects.

MAPKKKs consist of an N-terminal regulatory and a C-terminal catalytic kinase domain. The regulatory domain locks the C-terminal kinase domain in the inactive state. Activation can occur by phosphorylation through an upstream protein kinase or through interaction with other proteins, a process that often involves small G-proteins. The activation mechanisms and sensor systems upstream of the MAP kinase pathways are diverse, and include receptor-tyrosine kinase (in animal systems), G-protein coupled receptors, phosphorelay systems, and so on.

Different MAP kinase pathways form interacting signaling systems. For instance, one MAPKK may control several different MAP kinases, as is observed even in the relatively simple yeast system. Different pathways within the same organism often share kinases. Especially in higher eukaryotes, but even in *S. cerevisiae*, this situation results in highly complex network systems of signaling pathways. Pathway specificity is commonly, but probably not exclusively, achieved by scaffold proteins. Scaffold proteins may be apparently dedicated to this purpose, such as *S. cerevisiae* Ste5p, or may form part of the active components of the MAP kinase cascade, such as yeast MAPKK Pbs2p.

MAP kinase pathways are negatively controlled by protein phosphatases acting on both MAPKK and MAP kinase (serine–threonine phosphatases), or only on MAP kinase (tyrosine phosphatases).<sup>104)</sup>

*S. cerevisiae MAP kinase pathways.* Based on genetic analyses, the five MAP kinases are assigned to six distinct MAP kinase pathways: (i) the mating pheromone response pathway (MAP kinase Fus3p), (ii) the pseudohyphal development pathway (Kss1p), (iii) the high osmolarity glycerol pathway, HOG (Hog1p), (iv) the protein kinase C or cell integrity pathway (Slt2/Mpk1p), and (v) the spore wall assembly pathway (Smk1p).<sup>105–108)</sup> Components of the pheromone response pathway plus Sho1p are part of a distinct MAP kinase pathway, termed the STE vegetative growth pathway. The five MAP kinases are controlled by four MAPKKs, Ste7p, Pbs2p, the redundant Mkk1p and Mkk2p, and four MAPKKKs, Ste11p, Bck1p, and the redundant Ssk2p and Ssk22p.

*MAP kinase pathways in filamentous fungi.* Fungal genome sequences of the three *Aspergillus* species have revealed conserved and non-conserved aspects of MAP kinase pathways. While the numbers of MAPKK and MAPKKK are three of each throughout the three *Aspergillus* genome and the *N. crassa* genome, the numbers of MAPK are three for *N. crassa*, four for *A. nidulans* and *A. fumigatus*, and five for *A. oryzae*

(Fig. 7). Two types of putative phosphorylation sites (T-G-Y and T-E-Y) are found in fungal MAP kinases. The Hog1p ortholog (HogA) and its probable paralogs (MpkC and MpkD) have Thr-Gly-Tyr motifs (Figs. 7 and 8), although the functions of MpkC, D remain unclear. The Mpk1p ortholog (MpkA) and the Kss1p (or Fus3p) ortholog (MpkB) have the Thr-Glu-Tyr motif (Figs. 7 and 8). HOG genes appear to be redundant in the three *Aspergillus* species (Fig. 8). The three fungi appear to possess one MAPK kinase (MpkB), similar to either yeast Kss1p or Fus3p, but MpkB shows almost the same similarity to Kss1p and Fus3p (Fig. 8). This suggests that the signal transduction cascade of *A. oryzae* is the most complex of the four filamentous fungi. In the genus *Aspergillus*, only the HOG<sup>95,109–111)</sup> and cell integrity pathways<sup>112,113)</sup> are genetically characterized, and the others remain unclear.

(1) HOG MAP kinase cascade-osmotic stress response. In *S. cerevisiae*, external high-osmolarity activates the HOG (high-osmolarity glycerol) MAPK pathway (ScHOG), which consists of two upstream branches (Sln1p and Sho1p) and common downstream elements, including Pbs2p MAPKK and Hog1p MAPK. Activation of the pathway results in the induction of genes responsible for osmotic adaptation.<sup>103)</sup> Although the three *Aspergillus* species have all the counterparts of the ScHOG pathway in their genome (Fig. 2), the HOG

Genomics of Aspergillus oryzae 659

pathway has been genetically characterized only in *A. nidulans* (AnHOG), and hence we focus on the AnHOG pathway as representative of those of the three *Aspergillus* species.<sup>95)</sup> *A. nidulans hogAΔ* is not sensitive to high-osmolarity,<sup>110)</sup> and the null mutant of *tcsB*, which is the counterpart of yeast *SLN1* does not exhibit detectable phenotypes.<sup>95)</sup> These results suggest that *A. nidulans* has more complex and robust osmoregulatory systems than the ScHOG pathway, and that it has unknown high-osmolarity response pathways. *A. nidulans pbsB* gene encoding an ortholog of yeast Pbs2p MAPKK has been cloned and characterized.<sup>114)</sup> The *pbsB* gene suppresses the sensitivity of the yeast *pbs2* mutant to high-osmolarity, but it depends on the presence of Ssk2p/Ssk22p MAPKKKs. Although authentic *A. nidulans* PbsB MAPKK cannot suppress the sensitivity of the *ssk2Δ ssk22Δ pbs2Δ* triple mutant to high osmolarity, the fungal PbsB mutant containing the Pro-rich motif of *S. cerevisiae* Pbs2p (PbsB(Pro)) suppresses the phenotype. Hence, some of the most important connections between the Sho1p-Ste11p pathway and Pbs2p is not conserved in *A. nidulans*, and consequently, the ShoA-SteC pathway, which corresponds to the yeast Sho1p-Ste11p pathway, might not function as an osmosensor in *A. nidulans*. On the other hand, HogA MAPK in *A. nidulans sskAΔ* is not phosphorylated by increased external osmolarity. Therefore, the HogA MAPK can be activated only *via* the TcsB-YpdA-SskA "two-component" osmosensor, and not *via* the ShoA-SteC pathway.

SteC MAPKK of *A. nidulans* has the highest similarity to *N. crassa* Nrc-1, as it does to *S. cerevisiae* Ste11p.<sup>115)</sup> Deletion of the *steC* gene in *A. nidulans* results in a slower growth rate, formation of more branched hyphae, altered conidiophore morphology, and inhibition of heterokaryon formation and cleistothecium development. The *steC* gene is transcriptionally activated during asexual development and controls the phosphorylation of two putative MAP kinases.<sup>115)</sup> One predicted MAP kinase, with a molecular mass of 30 kDa, is phosphorylated during asexual development in a SteC-dependent manner. Its phosphorylation can be detected by the anti-phospho-p42/p44 antibody, which recognizes the tripeptide TEY, found in MpkA (predicted molecular mass, 47.8 kDa) and MpkB (41.6 kDa). Hence, Wei *et al.* have predicted that the 30 kDa protein is a novel MAP kinase that has not yet been assigned in the fungal genome sequences. Indeed, MpkA is required for spore germination and hyphal growth,<sup>112)</sup> and MpkB has not yet been functionally characterized. Wei *et al.* further examined whether some MAP kinases of *A. nidulans* were transiently phosphorylated under oxidative-stress conditions (H₂O₂). Phosphorylation of the 30 kDa protein detected with the anti-phospho-p42/p44 antibody and of a 49 kDa protein detected with the antiphospho-SAPK/JNK antibody, which recognizes the tripeptide TPY, was dependent on SteC under oxidative-stress conditions, despite the fact that the tripeptide TPY

is not found in any known *A. nidulans* MAP kinase. Identification of the SteC targets, as well as the discovery of other unknown MAP kinases involved in morphological transitions, is a goal of future research.

*A. fumigatus* also possesses the HOG pathway (Fig. 8).<sup>111)</sup> In *A. fumigatus*, HogA (SakA), which regulates conidial germination in response to the nitrogen source, is activated upon starvation of either carbon or nitrogen during vegetative growth.<sup>111)</sup>

(2) *Cell integrity pathway*. The cell wall of filamentous fungi is a complex structure essential to the maintenance of cell shape and integrity, prevention of cell lysis, and protection against environmental conditions. Fungal cells constantly remodel the rigid structure during growth and development, and under environmental stress.<sup>116)</sup> Proper cell wall architecture requires cell wall components such as $\beta$-1,3-glucan, $\beta$-1,6-glucan, chitin, and mannoproteins.<sup>117–119)</sup> Signal transduction that monitors the cell wall and promotes cell wall remodeling has been described in detail in the yeast *S. cerevisiae*.<sup>120)</sup> Sensing of cell wall perturbations requires surface sensors, which are encoded on *WSC* (cell wall integrity and stress response component) genes, upstream of the intracellular signal transduction pathway responsible for maintaining cell integrity in yeast. Wsc1-4p proteins are highly glycosylated plasma-membrane proteins containing an extracellular domain with a cysteine motif and an S/T-rich domain that carries glycosylation sites.<sup>121,122)</sup> Additional cell wall stress sensors are the partially redundant Mid2p and Mlt1p cell surface proteins. These proteins act as mechanosensors of cell wall stress during growth and pheromone-induced morphogenesis, high temperature, and other cell wall perturbations, and transmit the signals to the downstream signaling pathway.<sup>121,123)</sup> Activation of the cell integrity signaling pathway proceeds through the small G protein Rho1p *via* Pkc1p<sup>124)</sup> and a downstream MAP kinase cascade. Rho1p is a small GTPase upregulated by the GDP/GTP exchange factors Rom1p and Rom2p,<sup>125)</sup> and downregulated by the GTPase-activating proteins Sac7p and Bem2p.<sup>126)</sup> In addition to other functions, Rho1p binds and activates Pkc1p,<sup>127)</sup> which in turn activates the MAP kinase cascade. The MAP kinase cascade is a linear pathway composed of a MAPKKK (BCK1), a pair of redundant MAPKK (MKK1/2), and a MAP kinase (MPK1/SLT2).<sup>128–130)</sup> Cell integrity signaling is induced in response to several environmental stimuli, resulting in increased expression of numerous genes, many of which encode integral cell wall proteins (GPI proteins, PIR family proteins, and others) or enzymes involved in cell wall biogenesis, including $\beta$-1,3-glucan synthases (Fks1p, Fks2p) and chitin synthases.<sup>131)</sup>

Nevertheless, in yeast, a parallel cell integrity signaling mechanism involves the Ykr2p and Ypk1p kinases, and this signaling system is predicted to cross-talk with Pkc1p-Mpk1p cell integrity signaling.<sup>132)</sup> An additional alternative regulatory mechanism involved in cell wall

660 T. KOBAYASHI et al.

integrity is known as calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein phosphatase, calcineurin, dependent signaling.<sup>133)</sup> The role of calcineurin (Cna1/2p-Cnb1p) is mediated by the Crz1p zinc finger-containing transcription factor, which is dephosphorylated by calcineurin, and consequently binds to a promoter element called the calcineurin-dependent response element (CDRE). The *FKS2* gene, which encodes an alternative subunit of $\beta$-1,3-glucan synthase in addition to Fks1p, is a known target of Crz1p.<sup>134)</sup>

In filamentous fungi, including *A. nidulans* and *Magnaporthe grisea*, several genes encoding MAP kinases have been isolated.<sup>112,135)</sup> Deletion analysis of *A. nidulans mpkA*, a counterpart of yeast *MPK1* (*SLT2*), suggests that the kinase is involved in the germination of conidial spores and in polarized growth.<sup>112)</sup> However, no transcription factor that is directly involved in cell wall biogenesis has yet been isolated or characterized in filamentous fungi. The gene homologs involved in cell wall biogenesis have been identified *in silico* based on the three *Aspergillus* genome data sets (Fig. 8). Most homologs to those involved in yeast cell wall biogenesis are well conserved in the three fungi. It is noteworthy that the *fksA* gene coding for $\beta$-1,3-glucan synthase, and the *cnaA* gene coding for calcineurin, are not redundant genes in the three fungi, and that most cell wall biogenesis genes that include signaling components are also non-redundant. *In silico* assignment of transcription factors is generally difficult because conserved regions in transcription factors are often restricted to DNA binding domains such as a zinc finger domain and a leucine zipper motif. Other motifs are generally unavailable to distinguish transcription factors from each other. Fujioka et al. isolated the *A. nidulans rlmA* gene, which encodes a transcription factor with high similarity to yeast Rlm1p, using Rlm1p-specific signatures such as MADS (MCM1, Agamous, Deficients, SRF) box and an Mpk1p-docking region.<sup>113)</sup>

In *A. oryzae*, the cell integrity pathway has been analyzed using a morphologic mutant in which the *kexB* gene, encoding a subtilisin-like processing enzyme similar to *S. cerevisiae* Kex2p, was disrupted.<sup>113)</sup> The *kexB* disruptant ($\Delta$*kexB*) formed shrunken colonies with poor conidia generation on Czapek-Dox (CD) agar plates and hyperbranched mycelia in CD liquid medium. The phenotypes of the $\Delta$*kexB* strain were restored under high osmolarity under both solid and liquid culture conditions. Transcription of the *mpkA* gene, which encodes a putative mitogen-activated protein kinase involved in cell integrity signaling, was significantly higher in $\Delta$*kexB* cells than in wild-type cells. The $\Delta$*kexB* cells also contained higher levels of transcripts for cell wall-related genes encoding $\beta$-1,3-glucanosyltransferase and chitin synthases. This is presumably attributable to cell integrity signaling through the increased gene expression of *mpkA*. Constitutively increased levels of phosphorylated MpkA were also observed in $\Delta$*kexB* cells on the CD plate culture. High

osmotic stress remarkably downregulated the increased levels both of transcripts of *mpkA* gene and of the phosphorylated form of MpkA protein in $\Delta$*kexB*, concomitantly suppressing the morphological defects. These results suggest that the upregulation of transcription levels of *mpkA* and cell wall biogenesis genes in the $\Delta$*kexB* strain is autoregulated by phosphorylated MpkA as the activated form through cell integrity signaling. Taking this together, it is predicted that KexB is required for precise proteolytic processing of sensor proteins in the cell integrity pathway or of cell wall-related enzymes under transcriptional control by the pathway. Thus the KexB defect induces disordered cell integrity signaling.

Since analysis of the *A. oryzae* genome information indicates that some genes coding for signaling proteins upstream (histidine kinases [HK6, HK8], GPCRs, G$\alpha$ proteins) and downstream (5 MAPKs) are redundant, functional studies of the genes are necessary to determine how signaling systems are organized in the fungus.

# V. Protein Secretion

Among the variety of filamentous fungi, the importance of *Aspergillus* species for commercial use has recently increased, especially with regard to *A. oryzae*.<sup>136)</sup> Owing to its ability to secrete a wide variety of useful proteins and enzymes, it is also being manipulated genetically to enhance its heterologous protein production abilities.<sup>137)</sup> The fact that *A. oryzae* secretes a variety of proteins and enzymes in solid state fermentation<sup>138)</sup> makes it a very useful host in industrial applications. Hence an understanding of the genes responsible for the protein export mechanism is indispensable.

Proteins destined for secretion are essentially synthesized in the cytosol and must pass through membranes and organelles (such as the endoplasmic reticulum, ER, Golgi, etc.,) before being processed, and secreted into the exterior.<sup>139)</sup> The general mechanism attributed to this process involves coordination of a proteinaceous translocation network apparatus. However, our knowledge of the principles of the protein secretory machinery in filamentous fungi is still emerging, and thus several of the essential players involved in this complex pathway are as yet unknown. Obviously, one of the main challenges in research on protein secretion in filamentous fungi is critically to understand protein translocation at a molecular level, and hence genomics at this juncture might certainly be a powerful tool to reveal distinct clues towards deepening our understanding of the various elements of this protein export network. The recent completion of the *A. oryzae* genome sequencing project is expected to improve our knowledge of this extremely useful fungus and to aid in attempts to devise strategies to utilize it more efficiently in the production of proteins and enzymes.

The major hurdle underlying heterologous protein production and secretion in filamentous fungi is protein quality and turnover. Although efficient processing and folding of heterologous proteins is a primary role of the secretory system, misfolding of the proteins causes innate stress which in turn activates a process called the unfolded protein response (UPR) to maintain internal homeostasis.<sup>140)</sup> While some of the genes encoding proteins responsible for the translocation and processing of synthesized proteins in the ER, such as the foldases and chaperones, have been characterized in filamentous fungi, there appears to be a lacuna in terms of understanding the reasons behind the unimproved heterologous protein production system in some fungi<sup>139)</sup> even after overexpression of some of the components involved in proper protein maturation. The protein secretion pathway is therefore bound to be complex and may involve many additional components that make filamentous fungi more prolific secretors than the yeasts.

The protein secretory pathway in eukaryotes consists of several distinct organelles through which the trafficking of proteins occurs, and for this purpose, it is essential that these organelles possess a proper docking and fusion apparatus, which permits specific recognition of the approaching vesicles. It is well established that the transport of proteins is mediated by coated vesicles that bud off from membrane-bound compartments and are subsequently targeted to appropriate organelles through fusion events. Therefore, a highly specific and distinct combination of sensing factors facilitates ordered membrane targeting and fusion (e.g., ER to Golgi or Golgi to vacuole or Golgi to cell membranes, etc.). Several of these factors are collectively called SNARE regulators. They participate combinatorially in protein trafficking events.<sup>141)</sup> SNAREs (Soluble *N*-ethylmaleimide-sensitive fusion protein Attachment protein REceptors) are conserved membrane proteins present on vesicles (v-SNAREs) and target membranes (t-SNAREs). By interacting between each other they form the core of the vesicular targeting process and function in intracellular membrane fusion events. In general, SNARE

proteins consist of an alpha helical SNARE domain, which assembles with the other compatible domains (or factors including the Rab GTPases, AAA-type ATPases, and other tethering complexes) and provides the driving force for bilayer fusion. Helices of the SNARE domain can be divided into four classes: the Qa (syntaxin) class, the Qb (Bos1) class, the Qc (Bet1) class, and R-SNAREs.<sup>142)</sup> In filamentous fungi, SNAREs have important roles in hyphal tip growth and the secretion of extracellular enzymes. Gupta and Heath have reported SNAREs from genomes of filamentous fungi, including *N. crassa* and *A. fumigatus*.<sup>143)</sup> A comparative account of SNAREs in *A. oryzae* and other *Aspergillus* species, in addition to an overview of other important genes participating in the protein processing in *A. oryzae*, is presented.

## 1. Protein secretion pathway related genes in A. oryzae

The amino acid sequences of *S. cerevisiae* (SGD, http://genome-www.stanford.edu/Saccharomyces/) and *A. fumigatus* SNAREs<sup>143)</sup> were subjected to a Blastp search on the Manatee web site (http://www.tigr.org/tigr-scripts/proj/euk_manatee/shared/login.cgi). The ORF IDs with the highest hits are listed in Tables 7 and 8. When there were no obvious hits, a tblastn search was performed to find contigs containing homologous sequences. SNAREs were classified according to Pelham (2001).<sup>142)</sup>

Protein synthesis, targeting, and secretion involve a hierarchy of events. Following the synthesis of proteins, the quality-control aspects, such as processing, folding, and maturation, occur before the protein is functional or secreted. The various genes encoding ER resident chaperones (Bip, Hsp70, and calnexin homologs) and foldases (protein disulfide isomerases and peptidyl prolyl isomerase) for the quality control activity, apart from other secretion-pathway related genes, have been found in the genome of *A. oryzae* (Table 7). Among the three genes (AO090001000733, AO090001000733, and AO090003000829) classified as protein disulfide iso-

In addition, the yeast *ERO1* homolog reported to be essential for oxidative protein folding was also present in the *A. oryzae* genome (AO090005000630). *A. oryzae* also possessed three peptidyl-prolyl isomerase related genes (AO090023000811, AO090120000215, and AO090003001047), which contain an incomplete ER retention signal at their C-termini, casting doubt on their exact localization. Interestingly, the third peptidyl-prolyl isomerase (AO090003001047) was unique to *A. oryzae* among Aspergilli. A search for the Hsp70 family of genes that are known to assist in protein folding by protecting against oxygen deprivation in the *A. oryzae* genome showed the presence of one more ER resident Hsp70 (AO090005001222) in addition to the gene encoding BiP chaperone. In addition, the other homologs of genes encoding proteins required for the translocation of proteins into the ER, such as those belonging to the *SEC* family, were also identifiable in the *A. oryzae* genome (Table 8).

## 2. A comparative account of SNAREs in Aspergillus species

Most of the genes encoding SNAREs are equally distributed in the three Aspergilli and the sequences of SNARE domains are highly conserved, as in *N. crassa*.<sup>143)</sup> A list of the orthologs of SNAREs present in the three Aspergilli is shown in Table 9. No orthologs of Vam3 were found in the three Aspergilli genomes, confirming that it is specific to *S. cerevisiae* and *Candida albicans*.<sup>143)</sup> A single ortholog of *S. cerevisiae* Snc1 and Snc2, which are functionally redundant, was found in each Aspergillus. Another duplicated pair of SNAREs, Sso1 and Sso2, had a single counterpart in each Aspergillus. Interestingly, *A. oryzae* has an additional SNARE (AO070329000134), in which the SNARE domain shares homology with those of Sso SNAREs on plasma membranes, but the absolutely conserved glutamine residue in the central layer was replaced by histidine. Although according to the EST data, this gene (AO070329000134) was expressed in *A. oryzae* (AO1EST_SNGL0153, 1068) and also in *A. flavus* (TC5840), it is not yet clear whether this additional SNARE functions in *A. oryzae*. Other fungi such as *Magnaporthe grisea*, *Fusarium graminearum*,

*Cryptococcus neoformans*, and *Ustilago maydis* appear to contain two orthologs for Sso SNAREs with conserved glutamines. *N. crassa* also contains two Sso orthologs, NcSyn1 and NcSyn2.<sup>143)</sup> Both are involved in vegetative growth, but NcSyn2 perhaps has distinct roles in ascospore formation.<sup>145)</sup> *S. cerevisiae* Sso1, and not Sso2, is also required during sporulation,<sup>146)</sup> in conjunction with the sporulation-specific SNARE Spo20.<sup>147)</sup> Although there are no orthologs of the sporulation-specific SNARE Spo20, in all three Aspergilli and *N. crassa*, the role of Nsyn2 in ascospore formation hence indicates that the sporulation-specific SNARE complex is conserved in the fungal kingdom. The existence of an additional putative SNARE in *A. oryzae* suggests another exocytotic mechanism for the specific vesicle fusion step or, more likely, other (sexual) developmental stages in *A. oryzae*, although its sexual cycle has not yet been recognized. While the existence of almost all the homologs of genes encoding components of the protein secretion pathways of yeast in this group of filamentous fungi indicates a similar mechanism of secretion in operation, it is quite possible that filamentous fungi have additional components that enhance their protein production and secretion capabilities. The major difference is with reference to the polarized hyphal growth observed in fungi, which might be one factor contributing to higher potential for protein secretion.<sup>148)</sup> In general, it is thought that localization of SNAREs is stringently regulated in a specific and ordered fashion at each step of the secretory pathway. Hence a spatial distribution analysis of all the SNAREs in *A. oryzae* should not only elucidate the exact mechanism of establishing hyphal polarity via the secretory pathway, but should also help in the efficient use of this fungus in the production of important metabolites.

## VI. Conclusion

The genome sequence of *A. oryzae* has revealed striking metabolic diversity. This was overlooked for a long time perhaps because *A. oryzae* has been used mainly as a strong producer of amylases and proteases. The diversity obviously indicates the potential of the organism for further biotechnological applications as a source of many industrial enzymes other than amylases and proteases, as well as a number of primary and even secondary metabolites. It is a treasure house of enzymes and metabolites, and so the genome data should accelerate industrial application of the organism. *A. oryzae* has various beneficial characteristics for industrial application. It is a safe organism, and it secretes significant amounts of proteins, including heterologous ones. A great deal of information on *A. oryzae* cultures has been accumulated during the long history of industrial use of it in Japan, and a number of factories already exist to grow large masses of the organism. It might be unnecessary to look for other organisms to express hidden *A. oryzae* genes. *A. oryzae* will do it by itself if

R E V I E W Open Access
International Society of Sports Nutrition
Position Stand: protein and exercise
Ralf Jäger 1, Chad M. Kerksick 2, Bill I. Campbell 3, Paul J. Cribb 4, Shawn D. Wells 5, Tim M. Skwiat 5, Martin Purpura 1,
Tim N. Ziegenfuss 6, Arny A. Ferrando 7, Shawn M. Arent 8, Abbie E. Smith-Ryan 9, Jeffrey R. Stout 10, Paul J. Arciero 11,
Michael J. Ormsbee 12,13, Lem W. Taylor 14, Colin D. Wilborn 14, Doug S. Kalman 15, Richard B. Kreider 16,
Darryn S. Willoughby 17, Jay R. Hoffman 10, Jamie L. Krzykowski 18 and Jose Antonio 19*
Abstract
Position statement: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) provides an objective and critical review
related to the intake of protein for healthy, exercising individuals. Based on the current available literature, the
position of the Society is as follows:
1) An acute exercise stimulus, particularly resistance exercise, and protein ingestion both stimulate muscle protein
synthesis (MPS) and are synergistic when protein consumption occurs before or after resistance exercise.
2) For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance, an
overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4 –2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is sufficient for
most exercising individuals, a value that falls in line within the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range
published by the Institute of Medicine for protein.
3) There is novel evidence that suggests higher protein intakes (>3.0 g/kg/d) may have positive effects on body
composition in resistance-trained individuals (i.e., promote loss of fat mass).
4) Recommendations regarding the optimal protein intake per serving for athletes to maximize MPS are mixed
and are dependent upon age and recent resistance exercise stimuli. General recommendations are 0.25 g of a
high-quality protein per kg of body weight, or an absolute dose of 20 –40 g.
5) Acute protein doses should strive to contain 700 –3000 mg of leucine and/or a higher relative leucine content,
in addition to a balanced array of the essential amino acids (EAAs).
6) These protein doses should ideally be evenly distributed, every 3 –4 h, across the day.
7) The optimal time period during which to ingest protein is likely a matter of individual tolerance, since benefits
are derived from pre- or post-workout ingestion; however, the anabolic effect of exercise is long-lasting
(at least 24 h), but likely diminishes with increasing time post-exercise.

Background
In 2007, the International Society of Sports Nutrition
(ISSN) published its first position stand devoted to the
science and application of dietary protein intake [1].
Subsequently, this paper has been accessed more than
200,000 times and continues to serve as a key reference
on the topic. In the past ten years, there have been contin-
ued efforts to advance the science and application of diet-
ary protein intake for the benefit of athletes and fitness-
minded individuals. This updated position stand includes
new information and addresses the most important
dietary protein categories that affect physically active
individuals across domains such as exercise performance,
body composition, protein timing, recommended intakes,
protein sources and quality, and the preparation methods
of various proteins.
Benefits on exercise performance
Most of the scientific research investigating the effects
of protein intake on exercise performance has focused
on supplemental protein intake. From a broad perspec-
tive, the dependent measures of these studies can be
categorized into two domains:
/C15Endurance exercise performance
/C15Resistance exercise performance (increases in
maximal strength)
Endurance exercise performance
Very few studies have investigated the effects of
prolonged periods (one week or more) of dietary protein
manipulation on endurance performance. Macdermid
and colleagues [2] compared the influence of an isoener-
getic, high-protein/moderate-carbohydrate diet (3.3 and
5.9 g of protein and carbohydrate/kg body weight per day,
respectively) with a diet that was more typical of an
endurance athlete (1.3 and 7.9 g of protein and carbohy-
drate/kg body weight per day, respectively) in endurance-
trained cyclists. The trained cyclists ingested each diet for a
7-day period in a randomized, crossover fashion. Before
and following the 7-day diet intervention, a self-paced cyc-
ling endurance time trial was conducted as the primary
measure of exercise performance. At the end of the treat-
ment period, it took cyclists on the higher protein diet 20%
more time to complete the self-paced time trial - signifi-
cantly longer than for those on the lower protein/higher
carbohydrate diet. This finding is not surprising given that
dietary protein is not a preferred energy source and the
dietary carbohydrate intakes in the higher protein treat-
ment were below recommended intakes for endurance ath-
letes (6–10 g of carbohydrate/kg/d) [3]. It should be noted
however that a 7-day treatment period is exceedingly brief.
It is unknown what the effect of a higher protein diet would
be over the course of several weeks or months.
In another study [4] utilizing highly trained cyclists dur-
ing a period of increased training intensity, it was ob-
served that 3 g of protein/kg/d offered no improvements
in a simulated time trial as compared to 1.5 g of protein/
kg body weight/day. Carbohydrate intake was kept con-
stant (6 g/kg/d) in both the moderate and high protein
treatments during this three-week intervention. Although
the number of investigations is limited, it appears as if in-
creasing protein intakes above recommended intakes does
not enhance endurance performance [2, 4, 5].
In addition to these studies that spanned one to three
weeks, several acute-response (single feeding and exercise
sessions) studies exist, during which protein was added to a
carbohydrate beverage prior to or during endurance exercise.
Similarly, most of these interventions also reported no added
improvements in endurance performance when protein was
added to a carbohydrate beverage as compared to carbohy-
drate alone [6–9]. An important research design note, how-
ever, is that those studies which reported improvements in
8) While it is possible for physically active individuals to obtain their daily protein requirements through the
consumption of whole foods, supplementation is a practical way of ensuring intake of adequate protein quality
and quantity, while minimizing caloric intake, particularly for athletes who typically complete high volumes of
training.
9) Rapidly digested proteins that contain high proportions of essential amino acids (EAAs) and adequate leucine,
are most effective in stimulating MPS.
10) Different types and quality of protein can affect amino acid bioavailability following protein
supplementation.
11) Athletes should consider focusing on whole food sources of protein that contain all of the EAAs (i.e., it is the
EAAs that are required to stimulate MPS).
12) Endurance athletes should focus on achieving adequate carbohydrate intake to promote optimal performance;
the addition of protein may help to offset muscle damage and promote recovery.
13) Pre-sleep casein protein intake (30 –40 g) provides increases in overnight MPS and metabolic rate
without influencing lipolysis.
Jäger et al. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (2017) 14:20 Page 2 of 25

endurance performance when protein was added to a carbo-
hydrate beverage before and during exercise all used a time-
to-exhaustion test [10–12]. When specifically interested in
performance outcomes, a time trial is preferred as it better
mimics competition and pacing demands.
In conclusion, added protein does not appear to im-
prove endurance performance when given for several
days, weeks, or immediately prior to and during endur-
ance exercise. While no ergogenic outcomes may be evi-
dent, the scientific literature is consistent in reporting that
adding protein to a carbohydrate beverage/gel during ex-
haustive endurance exercise suppresses markers of muscle
damage (creatine kinase) 12 to 24 h post-exercise [8, 11 –
13] and decreases the endurance athletes ’ feelings of mus-
cular soreness [6 –8, 13]. For these reasons, it seems pru-
dent to recommend for endurance athletes to ingest
approximately 0.25 g of protein/kg body weight per hour
of endurance exercise (in addition to the athlete ’sr e g u l a r
carbohydrate intake) to suppress markers of muscle dam-
age and improve subjective feelings of muscular soreness
[11, 12]. Another important consideration relates to the
impact of ingesting protein along with carbohydrate on
rates of protein synthesis and balance during prolonged
bouts of endurance exercise. Beelen and colleagues [14]
determined that adding protein to carbohydrate consump-
tion throughout a prolonged bout of endurance exercise
promotes a higher whole body net protein balance, but
the added protein does not exert any further impact on
rates of MPS. While performance outcomes were not
measured, these results shift the focus of nutrient inges-
tion during prolonged bouts of endurance exercise to the
ingestion of carbohydrate.
Key points
/C15When adequate carbohydrate is delivered, adding
protein to carbohydrate does not appear to improve
endurance performance over the course of a few
days or weeks.
/C15Adding protein during or after an intensive bout of
endurance exercise may suppress the rise in plasma
proteins linked to myofibrillar damage and reduce
feelings of muscle soreness.
/C15There are relatively few investigations on the effects
of protein supplementation on endurance
performance.
Resistance exercise performance
The extent to which protein supplementation, in
conjunction with resistance training, enhances maximal
strength is contingent upon many factors, including:
/C15Resistance-training program variables
(such as intensity, volume, and progression)
/C15Length of the resistance-training program/
intervention
/C15Training status of the participants engaging in the
resistance-training program
/C15Energy intake in the diet
/C15Quality and quantity of protein intake (with an
emphasis on leucine content of the protein)
/C15Co-ingestion of additional dietary ingredients that
may favorably impact strength (e.g. creatine, HMB)
Taking each of these variables into consideration, the
effects of supplemental protein consumption has on
maximal strength enhancement are varied, with a majority
of the investigations reporting no benefit [15 –25] and a
few reporting improvements in maximal strength [26 –29].
With limited exceptions [16, 18, 23, 27], most of the stud-
ies utilized young, healthy, untrained males as partici-
pants. In one investigation examining college football
athletes supplementing with a proprietary milk protein
supplement (two servings of 42 g per day) for 12 weeks, a
14.5% increase in maximal squat strength was observed
compared to a 6.9% increase in the placebo group [28].
These differences were statistically significant. When
females were the only sex investigated, the outcomes
consistently indicated that supplemental protein does not
appear to enhance maximal strength at magnitudes that
reach statistical significance. Hida et al. [30] reported that
females supplementing with 15 g of egg white protein
(which raised daily protein intake to 1.23 g of protein/kg
body weight/day) experienced no improvements in max-
imal upper and lower body strength as compared to a
carbohydrate placebo (ingesting one gram of protein/kg
body weight/day) over an 8-week period. An important
note for this study is that 15 g of egg protein is considered
by many to be a sub-optimal dose [31]. However, others
have advocated that the total daily intake of protein might
be as important or more important [32]. In another study,
Josse et al. [33] reported that non-resistance trained fe-
males supplementing with one liter of skimmed bovine
milk (providing 36 g of protein) after resistance exercise
improved maximal strength in seven of nine measures as
compared to a carbohydrate placebo group, but only the
improvements to maximal bench press strength attained
statistical significance compared to the placebo. In
contrast, T aylor and colleagues [34] reported that pre- and
post-exercise whey protein ingestion significantly in-
creased maximal upper-body strength (+4.9 kg bench
press one repetition maximum) in comparison to changes
seen when a maltodextrin placebo (+2.3 kg) was ingested
in a group of female collegiate basketball players over an
8-week period.
In summary, while research investigating the addition
of supplemental protein to a diet with adequate energy
and nutrient intakes is inconclusive in regards to
Jäger et al. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (2017) 14:20 Page 3 of 25

stimulating strength gains in conjunction with a
resistance-training program to a statistically significant
degree, greater protein intakes that are achieved from
both dietary and supplemental sources do appear to have
some advantage. Hoffman and colleagues [29] reported
that in athletes consuming daily protein intakes above
2.0 g/kg/d which included protein intakes from both diet
and supplements, a 22% and 42% increase in strength
was noted in both the squat and bench press exercises
during off-season conditioning in college football players
compared to athletes that consumed only the recom-
mended levels (1.6 –1.8 g/kg/d) for strength/power
athletes. Further, it is important to highlight that in most
studies cited, protein intervention resulted in greater but
non-statistically significant strength improvements as
compared to the placebo/control condition. Cermak and
colleagues [35] pooled the outcomes from 22 separate
clinical trials to yield 680 subjects in their statistical
analysis and found that protein supplementation with
resistance training resulted in a 13.5 kg increase (95%
Confidence Interval: 6.4 –20.7 kg) in lower-body strength
when compared to changes seen when a placebo was
provided. A similar conclusion was also drawn by
Pasiakos et al. [36] in a meta-analysis where they
reported that in untrained participants, protein sup-
plementation might exert very little benefit on
strength during the initial weeks of a resistance train-
ing program, but as duration, frequency and volume
of resistance training increased, protein supplementa-
tion may favorably impact skeletal muscle hyper-
trophy and strength.
Key points:
/C15Results from many single investigations indicate that
in both men and women protein supplementation
exerts a small to modest impact on strength
development.
/C15Pooled results of multiple studies using meta-analytic
and other systematic approaches consistently indicate
that protein supplementation (15 to 25 g over 4 to
21 weeks) exerts a positive impact on performance.
Body composition
Improving one ’s body composition through the loss of
fat mass and increasing fat-free mass is often associated
with improvements in physical performance. In this re-
spect, many published investigations report that protein
supplementation results in significant improvements in
lean body weight/cross-sectional areas as compared to
placebo treatments [15, 17, 21 –23, 26, 27, 33, 37].
Andersen et al. [15] examined 22 healthy men that
completed a 14-week resistance-training program
(3 days/week consisting of 3 –4 sets of lower body
exercises) while supplementing with either 25 g of a
high-quality protein blend or 25 g of carbohydrate.
When the blend of milk proteins was provided, signifi-
cantly greater increases in fat-free mass, muscle cross-
sectional area in both the Type I and Type II muscle
fibers occurred when compared to changes seen with
carbohydrate consumption. Collectively, a meta-analysis
by Cermak and colleagues [35] reported a mean increase
in fat-free mass of 0.69 kg (95% Confidence Interval:
0.47–0.91 kg) when protein supplementation was
provided versus a placebo during a resistance-training
program. Other reviews by Tipton, Phillips and Pasiakos,
respectively, [36, 38, 39] provide further support that
protein supplementation (15 –25 g over 4 –14 weeks)
augments lean mass accretion when combined with
completion of a resistance training program.
Beyond accretion of fat-free mass, increasing daily
protein intake through a combination of food and
supplementation to levels above the recommended daily
allowance (RDA) (RDA 0.8 g/kg/day, increasing to 1.2 –
2.4 g/kg/day for the endurance and strength/power ath-
letes) while restricting energy intake (30 –40% reduction
in energy intake) has been demonstrated to maximize
the loss of fat tissue while also promoting the mainten-
ance of fat-free mass [40 –45]. The majority of this work
has been conducted using overweight and obese individ-
uals who were prescribed an energy-restricted diet that
delivered a greater ratio of protein relative to carbohy-
drate. As a classic example, Layman and investigators
[40] randomized obese women to consume one of two
restricted energy diets (1600 –1700 kcals/day) that were
either higher in carbohydrates (>3.5: carbohydrate-to-
protein ratio) or protein (<1.5: carbohydrate-to-protein ra-
tio). Groups were further divided into those that followed
a five-day per week exercise program (walking + resistance
training, 20 –50 min/workout) and a control group that
performed light walking of less than 100 min per week.
Greater amounts of fat were lost when higher amounts of
protein were ingested, but even greater amounts of fat loss
occurred when the exercise program was added to the
high-protein diet group, resulting in significant decreases
in body fat. Using an active population that ranged from
normal weight to overweight (BMI: 22 –29 kg/m 2),
Pasiakos and colleagues [42] examined the impact of pro-
gressively increasing dietary protein over a 21-day study
period. An aggressive energy reduction model was
employed that resulted in each participant reducing their
caloric intake by 30% and increasing their energy expend-
iture by 10%. Each person was randomly assigned to
consume a diet that contained either 1× (0.8 g/kg), 2×
(1.6 g/kg) or 3× (2.4 g/kg) the RDA for protein. Partici-
pants were measured for changes in body weight and body
composition. While the greatest body weight loss occurred
in the 1× RDA group, this group also lost the highest
Jäger et al. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (2017) 14:20 Page 4 of 25

percentage of fat-free mass and lowest percentage of fat
mass. The 2× and 3× RDA groups lost significant amounts
of body weight that consisted of 70% and 64% fat mass,
respectively.
Collectively, these results indicate that increasing
dietary protein can promote favorable adaptations in
body composition through the promotion of fat-free
mass accretion when combined with a hyperenergetic
diet and a heavy resistance training program and can
also promote the loss of fat mass when higher intakes of
daily protein (2-3× the RDA) are combined with an
exercise program and a hypoenergetic diet.
Key points:
/C15When combined with a hyperenergetic diet and a
heavy resistance-training program, protein
supplementation may promote increases in skeletal
muscle cross-sectional area and lean body mass.
/C15When combined with a resistance-training program
and a hypoenergetic diet, an elevated daily intake of
protein (2 – 3× the RDA) can promote greater
losses of fat mass and greater overall improvements
in body composition.
Protein timing
Thanks to seminal work by pioneering research groups
[37, 46, 47], by the 1990 ’s it was clear that exercise and
macronutrient consumption interact synergistically to
provide a net anabolic effect far greater than either feed-
ing or exercise alone. In the absence of feeding, muscle
protein balance remains negative in response to an acute
bout of resistance exercise [48]. Tipton et al. [49] were
one of the first groups to illustrate that an acute feeding
of amino acids significantly increases rates of muscle
protein synthesis (MPS). Later, Burd et al. [50] indicated
that the combination of acute, exhaustive resistance
exercise increases the muscle ’s anabolic responsiveness
to whey protein provision for up to 24 h. In addition to
heightened anabolic sensitivity that stems from the
combination of resistance exercise and protein/amino
acid feeding, the importance of the EAAs with respect
to muscle protein growth has also been elucidated.
Tipton et al. [51] first indicated that nonessential amino
acids were not necessary to stimulate MPS. Subse-
quently, these conclusions were supported by Borsheim
[52] and Volpi [53]. The study by Borsheim also docu-
mented a dose-response outcome characterized by a
near doubling of net protein balance in response to a
three to six gram dose of the EAAs [52]. Building on this
work, Tipton et al. [54] reported that EAAs (9 –15 g
dose) before and after resistance exercise promoted
higher net protein accretion, not just 3 or 4 h post exer-
cise but also over a 24-h period [55]. These findings
formed the theoretical concept of protein timing for
resistance exercise that has since been transferred to not
only other short-duration, high-intensity activities [56]
but also endurance-based sports [57] and subsequent
performance outcomes [58]. The strategic consumption
of nutrition, namely protein or various forms of amino
acids, in the hours immediately before and during
exercise (i.e., peri-workout nutrition) has been shown to
maximize muscle repair and optimize strength- and
hypertrophy-related adaptations [59, 60]. While earlier
investigations reported positive effects from consump-
tion of amino acids [37, 46, 61], it is now clear that
intact protein supplements such as egg, whey, casein,
beef, soy and even whole milk can evoke an anabolic
response that can be similar or greater in magnitude
to free form amino acids, assuming ingestion of equal
EAA amounts [62 –64].
For instance, whey protein ingested close to resistance
exercise, promotes a higher activation (phosphorylation)
of mTOR (a key signaling protein found in myocytes
that is linked to the synthesis of muscle proteins) and its
downstream mRNA translational signaling proteins (i.e.,
p70s6 kinase and eIF4BP) that further suggests timed in-
gestion of protein may favorably promote heightened
muscle hypertrophy [21, 62]. Moreover, it was found that
the increased mTOR signaling corresponded with
significantly greater muscle hypertrophy after 10 weeks
of training [65]. However, the hypertrophic differences
between protein consumption and a non-caloric placebo
appeared to plateau by week 21, despite a persistently
greater activation of this molecular signaling pathway
from supplementation. Results from other research
groups [56 –58, 66] show that timing of protein near
(± 2 h) aerobic and anaerobic exercise training ap-
pears to provide a greater activation of the molecular
signalling pathways that regulate myofibrillar and
mitochondrial protein synthesis as well as glycogen
synthesis.
It is widely reported that protein consumption directly
after resistance exercise is an effective way to acutely
promote a positive muscle protein balance [31, 55, 67],
which if repeated over time should translate into a net
gain or hypertrophy of muscle [68]. Pennings and col-
leagues [69] reported an increase in both the delivery
and incorporation of dietary proteins into the skeletal
muscle of young and older adults when protein was
ingested shortly after completion of exercise. These
findings and others add to the theoretical basis for
consumption of post-protein sooner rather than later
after exercise, since post workout MPS rates peak within
three hours and remain elevated for an additional 24 –
72 h [50, 70]. This extended time frame also provides a
rationale for both immediate and sustained (i.e., every
3–4 h) feedings to optimize impact. These temporal
Jäger et al. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (2017) 14:20 Page 5 of 25

considerations would also capture the peak elevation in
signalling proteins shown to be pivotal for increasing the
initiation of translation of muscle proteins, which for the
most part appears to peak between 30 and 60 min after
exercise [71]. Finally, while some investigations have
shown that a rapid increase in amino acids (aminoacide-
mia) from a protein dose immediately after or surround-
ing exercise stimulates increased adaptations to resistance
training [72, 73], others examining competitive strength/
power athletes reported no advantage from pre/post sup-
plement feedings compared to similar feedings in morning
and evening hours [74]. However, these differences may
be related to the type of protein used between the studies.
The studies showing positive effects of protein timing
used milk proteins, whereas the latter study used a colla-
gen based protein supplement.
While a great deal of work has focused on post-
exercise protein ingestion, other studies have suggested
that pre-exercise and even intra-exercise ingestion may
also support favorable changes in MPS and muscle
protein breakdown [14, 54, 75 –78]. Initially, Tipton and
colleagues [54] directly compared immediate pre-
exercise and immediate post-exercise ingestion of a mix-
ture of carbohydrate (35 g) and EAAs (6 g) combination
on changes in MPS. They reported that pre-exercise
ingestion promoted higher rates of MPS while also
demonstrating that nutrient ingestion prior to exercise
increased nutrient delivery to a much greater extent
than other (immediate or one hour post-exercise)
time points. These results were later challenged by
Fujita in 2009 who employed an identical study de-
sign with a different tracer incorporation approach
and concluded there was no difference between pre-
or post-exercise ingestion [75]. Subsequent work by
Tipton [79] also found that similar elevated rates of
MPS were achieved when ingesting 20 g of a whey
protein isolate immediately before or immediately
after resistance exercise.
At this point, whether any particular time of protein
ingestion confers any unique advantage over other time
points throughout a 24-h day to improve strength and
hypertrophy has yet to be adequately investigated. To
date, although a substantial amount of literature dis-
cusses this concept [60, 80], a limited number of training
studies have assessed whether immediate pre- and post-
exercise protein consumption provides unique advan-
tages compared to other time points [72, 73, 81]. Each
study differed in population, training program, environ-
ment and nutrition utilized, with each reporting a
different result. What is becoming clear is that the
subject population, nutrition habits, dosing protocols on
both training and non-training days, energy and macro-
nutrient intake, as well as the exercise bout or training
program itself should be carefully considered alongside
the results. In particular, the daily amount of protein intake
seems to operate as a key consideration because the bene-
fits of protein timing in relation to the peri-workout period
seem to be lessened for people who are already ingesting
appropriate amounts of protein (e.g. ≥1.6 g/kg/day). This
observation can be seen when comparing the initial
results of Cribb [72], Hoffman [74] and most recently
with Schoenfeld [82]; however, one must also consider
that the participants in the Hoffman study may have
been hypocaloric as they reported consuming approxi-
mately 30 kcal/kg in all groups across the entire
study. A literature review by Aragon and Schoenfeld
[83] determined that while compelling evidence exists
showing muscle is sensitized to protein ingestion
following training, the increased sensitivity to protein
ingestion might be greatest in the first five to six
hours following exercise. Thus, the importance of
timing may be largely dependent on when a pre-
workout meal was consumed, the size and compos-
ition of that meal and the total daily protein in the
diet. In this respect, a pre-exercise meal will provide
amino acids during and after exercise and therefore it
stands to reason there is less need for immediate
post-exercise protein ingestion if a pre-exercise meal
is consumed less than five hours before the antici-
pated completion of a workout. A meta-analysis by
Schoenfeld et al. [84] found that consuming protein
within one-hour post resistance exercise had a small
but significant effect on increasing muscle hyper-
trophy compared to delaying consumption by at least
two hours. However, sub-analysis of these results re-
